newsitem.title: USA: Fortified foods make inroads on global nutrition.
newsitem.headline: Fortified foods make inroads on global nutrition.

text.p: Dramatic success in nations like Guatemala, Venezuela, the Philippines and Thailand shows the world can overcome nutrient shortages in food that are to blame for millions of deaths and illnesses, health experts said on Wednesday.

More than one billion people suffer from mild micronutrient malnutrition, mainly lack of sufficient iodine, iron and vitamin A. Advocates call the situation a "hidden hunger" because the deficiencies are not immediately obvious but can result in mental retardation, night blindness, lower intelligence levels and lower productivity.

"The tragedy is this need not exist," M.G. Venkatesh Mannar, executive director of the Micronutrient Initiative, said in an interview in advance of a conference on Saturday in Montreal to discuss progress and to plan new projects.
"Here is a chance to make a major impact at a fairly low cost that does not rely greatly on government investment."

World leaders pledged at the start of the decade to try to eliminate micronutrient malnutrition this decade. Appeals to iodize salt worldwide have been widely adopted. More than $1 billion has been donated toward that goal.

Public health experts said it was inexpensive to fortify foods with micronutrients. Key was finding a suitable, widely consumed food and forging a government and industry alliance to carry out the plan. Beneficial results appeared quickly with fortified foods.

In Venezuela, it costs about 10 cents per person per year to add iron and vitamins to wheat and corn flour, said Jose Chavez Perez, of the National Institute of Nutrition. Iron deficiency and anaemia has been cut 60 percent.
Omar Dary of the Panamerican Health Organisation said Guatemala reduced vitamin A deficiency by half in two years by fortifying sugar, used in making many foods.

In the Philippines, vitamin A deficiency was cut by two-thirds among children by fortifying a popular, low-priced brand of margarine, said Florentino Solon, executive director of the Nutrition Centre of the Philippines. Iodine has been added to salt, he said, and now bread was being fortified with iron and vitamin A.
In Thailand, iodine, iron and vitamin A were added to seasoning packets for instant noodles, a staple of the Thai diet, to reduce child mortality.
Iron deficiency causes one-half of all types of anaemia, which is a leading cause of death for the one-half million women who die in childbirth each year.
Lack of iodine can permanently reduce children's IQs by 10 points. Some 655 million people suffer from goiter, a swelling of the thyroid gland caused by iodine deficiency.
Vitmain A deficiency impairs vision and was estimated to blind up to 500,000 children a year, two-thirds of whom die shortly afterwards.
